sermon:
## Is There No God in Israel?
*When a broken man sends past the LORD to ask a foreign god the only question that matters*

**Text:** 2 Kings 1–2 · **Supporting:** 1 Kings 18:21 · Deuteronomy 18:15 · 2 Kings 2:9 · 2 Kings 2:14

Ahaziah fell through a lattice in his upper chamber and lay there with his bones broken, and the first thing he reached for was a god in another country. Not the God of his fathers. Not the God who had answered fire on Carmel in his own father's lifetime. He sent messengers to Ekron, to Baal-zebub, the lord of the flies — the god of the Philistines, the enemy. A king of Israel, hurt and afraid, looking everywhere but home.

**A king who would consult anyone but the LORD**

The text does not let us soften it. "Go, inquire of Baal-zebub the god of Ekron, whether I shall recover of this disease" (2 Kings 1:2). This is the deathbed of a man who has had a whole life to know better and has decided, at the edge of the grave, that the God of Israel is one option among several — and not the most convenient one. Baal-zebub asks nothing of him. The God of Sinai asks everything. So he sends past Him.

The LORD's answer comes through Elijah, and it lands as a question that pins the king to the wall: "Is it not because there is no God in Israel, that ye go to inquire of Baal-zebub the god of Ekron?" (2 Kings 1:3). The question is not about geography. It is about ownership. The God who made covenant with this nation, who carried it out of Egypt, who set His name on this people — that God is being treated as if He were absent or insufficient. Elijah's father in the faith had already framed the choice on Carmel: "How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him" (1 Kings 18:21). Ahaziah is the proof that a man can witness the fire and still hedge his bets.

Fifty soldiers come to fetch the prophet, and fire falls. Then fifty more, and fire falls again. We recoil — and we should sit in the discomfort rather than explain it away. The third captain comes on his knees, begging for his life, and is spared. The judgment is not arbitrary cruelty. It is the LORD refusing to be summoned and managed by a king who would not consult Him about his own dying body. You cannot send past God and then command His prophet down a hill at sword-point. The God of Israel will not be one god among many, available when convenient and ignored when costly.

**A mantle that falls on a servant**

Then the chapter turns to a parting. Elijah knows he is leaving, and Elisha will not let him go alone. Three times Elijah tells him to stay, and three times Elisha answers, "As the LORD liveth, and as thy soul liveth, I will not leave thee" (2 Kings 2:2). They cross the Jordan on dry ground, the master strikes the water with his mantle and it parts — the same water that opened for Joshua, the God of the exodus still at work. And Elisha asks for the one thing worth asking: "I pray thee, let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me" (2 Kings 2:9).

Not Elijah's fame. Not his platform. His spirit — the Spirit of the LORD that made the man a prophet at all. The chariot of fire comes, the whirlwind takes Elijah up alive, and the mantle falls to the ground. Elisha picks it up, walks back to the river, and strikes the water with the dead man's cloak, asking, "Where is the LORD God of Elijah?" (2 Kings 2:14). The Jordan parts again. The God who answered the master answers the servant. The point is not the magic of a mantle. The point is that the God of Israel is still God when the great man is gone, and the word does not depend on the one who carried it.

**The God who will not be one option among many**

Now turn around, because we are Ahaziah more often than we will admit. We do not send to Ekron. We send to the diagnosis, the financial plan, the second opinion, the strong man who promises to keep us safe — and we send to God last, if at all, and mostly to confirm what we already decided. I have done this. I have lain in my own broken places and reached for every consolation before I reached for the One who made me, and I have done it knowing better, which is the whole horror of it. The question Elijah asks the king, God asks the church. Is there no God in Israel, that you inquire of everything else first?

This is the book of 2 Kings opening its mouth. A kingdom is going to die slowly across these chapters because it kept treating the covenant God as optional. And yet — hold this — the same God who will not be consulted as one among many is the God who takes a faithful man up alive in a chariot of fire, and who answers the trembling servant at the river. The judgment and the mercy come from the same hand. The exile that is coming and the ember of grace that survives it both flow from a God who insists on being God.

Every failed son of David in this book is reaching for a foreign comfort while the true comfort stands waiting. And the prophet greater than Elijah, the one whose mantle is His own Spirit poured out, would one day cross His own dark Jordan, taken up not before death but through it, so that the question "Is there no God in Israel" could be answered for good at an empty tomb. The LORD God of Elijah is still asking. He will not be your last resort.

Ask Israel's God, or none.

## The God of Armies and the God of the Kitchen
*Water in the wilderness, oil in the widow's house, and the LORD who provides where you ran dry*

**Text:** 2 Kings 3–4 · **Supporting:** 2 Kings 3:17 · 2 Kings 4:6 · 2 Kings 4:43 · Matthew 6:11

Three kings march an army into a desert and run out of water on the third day. Edom, Judah, and faithless Israel, all of them stranded between the campaign and the grave, with no spring and no plan. And the king of Israel does what frightened men do — he blames God for the thing his own faithlessness made likely. The whole chapter turns on a question of provision, and the answer comes not from a well but from a word.

**The word that fills a dry valley**

Jehoshaphat, the one decent man among the three, asks the only useful question: "Is there not here a prophet of the LORD?" (2 Kings 3:11). Elisha is found, and he is blunt — were it not for the godly king of Judah, he would not so much as look at the king of Israel. Then he speaks, and the word of the LORD reorders the desert: "Ye shall not see wind, neither shall ye see rain; yet that valley shall be filled with water" (2 Kings 3:17). No storm. No visible cause. The trenches fill in the night, and at dawn the sun on the water looks like blood to the enemy, and the battle is won by provision the army never produced.

This is the first thing 2 Kings wants us to learn about the LORD before the kingdom falls: He provides where there is no mechanism for provision. Not because the people deserved it — this army is led by a son of Ahab, a king the prophet would not have crossed the room for — but because His word is enough to fill a valley. The God of armies is real. He gives the victory. But notice where the chapter has been pointing: not to the strength of the kings, who had none, not to the cleverness of their campaign, which had stranded them, but to the word of the prophet, which had everything. The deliverance does not come down the chain of command. It comes down from heaven, through a man no king could control, to an army that had run itself dry.

**The God who fills the widow's empty jars**

Then the camera moves from the battlefield to the kitchen, and it stays there. A widow comes to Elisha, her husband dead, the creditor at the door to take her two sons as slaves. What do you have in the house? A pot of oil. Borrow vessels, shut the door, pour. And the oil flows until the last borrowed jar is full and there is not one more to fill: "And it came to pass, when the vessels were full... there is not a vessel more. And the oil stayed" (2 Kings 4:6). The provision ran exactly as far as her faith reached for vessels and stopped.

The Shunammite woman builds the prophet a room, is given the son she never asked for, and watches him die in her lap on a noonday with no warning. She saddles a donkey, rides hard to the man of God, and will not be put off with a staff sent ahead by a servant — she wants the prophet himself, falls at his feet, and holds him to it, and God raises the boy and gives him back alive into her arms. A pot of stew is poisoned, death in the pot, the sons of the prophets afraid to eat, and a handful of meal makes it safe. A hundred men are fed from twenty barley loaves in a famine, and there is bread left over, "according to the word of the LORD" (2 Kings 4:43). The God who filled the desert valley fills the widow's jars and the dead boy's lungs and the hungry men's hands. The same God. The same word. The God who can rout a foreign army can also pay a poor woman's debt and raise her only child, and He counts neither beneath Him.

**Where you ran dry**

We are quick to believe God runs the armies and slow to believe He runs the kitchen. We trust Him with the campaign and carry the household alone — the unpaid bill, the empty pantry, the child we cannot raise back to life. I have sat with widows in my own office who believed God was big enough for the nation and far too busy for their rent, and I have preached a God of armies on Sunday and lived as a practical atheist about my own dry Tuesday, so I am not describing someone else. The book of 2 Kings will not let us split God in two. The God who fills valleys fills jars. The God of the battle is the God of the bread.

And here is the weight. This kingdom is sliding toward exile because it would not trust the God who provides; it ran to Egypt and Assyria and Baal for the water it could have had from His word. The miracles of mercy in these chapters — the oil, the raised son, the cleansed pot, the multiplied loaves — are not a contradiction of the coming judgment. They are the patience inside it. God kept providing for a people running dry by their own choosing, kept sending the word that would have saved them, long after they stopped asking.

The widow's oil and the multiplied loaves run straight to a hillside where the prophet greater than Elisha would break bread for thousands and gather up what was left over — the same provision, the same word made flesh, teaching a starving people to ask, "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11). And that prophet would go into the exile we earned, down into the death that swallows widows' sons, so that the God who fills empty jars could fill an empty tomb and pour out provision on a people who deserved the desert. He is the God of the kitchen. He has not forgotten your dry day.

He provides where you ran dry.

## Wash and Be Clean
*The pride that almost walked away from grace, and the greed that carried the leprosy home*

**Text:** 2 Kings 5 · **Supporting:** 2 Kings 5:11 · 2 Kings 5:13 · 2 Kings 5:14 · Ephesians 2:8

Naaman was a great man. Commander of the armies of Syria, honorable, mighty, a deliverer of his nation — and a leper. The text stacks the titles high and then sets the disease at the bottom of the list like a stone, and the weight of the whole chapter is in that arrangement. Greatness on top. Death underneath. And the cure, when it comes, is going to offend him before it heals him.

**Healing on his own terms**

The word reaches him through a captured Israelite slave girl, of all people — a child stolen in a raid, who pities her master and points him to a prophet in Samaria. Naaman comes the way great men come, with horses and chariots and silver and a letter from his king, ready to purchase his healing at a fair price. And Elisha will not even come to the door. He sends a messenger: go wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh will come again.

Naaman is furious. "Behold, I thought, He will surely come out to me, and stand, and call on the name of the LORD his God, and strike his hand over the place, and recover the leper" (2 Kings 5:11). He had the whole healing scripted — the ceremony he deserved, the dignity owed a man of his rank, the impressive gesture. And he got a muddy river and a message passed through a servant. Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? His own country had cleaner water. If the cure is this plain, this beneath him, this free, he would rather keep his leprosy with his pride intact.

This is the offense of grace, and it has not changed. Grace does not come to the great man as a transaction he can manage. It comes as a command he must obey, in a form he did not choose, that strips him of every reason to be proud of his own healing. Naaman wanted to be cured as a commander. He had to be cured as a leper — which is to say, as a man with nothing to offer and nowhere to go but down into the dirty water. The silver in his saddlebags could buy nothing here. The letter from his king carried no weight here. The whole apparatus of his greatness, which had bought him everything else in life, could not buy him one clean inch of skin. That is what enrages him: not the difficulty of the cure, but the way it makes his greatness irrelevant.

**The bend, the wash, the clean flesh**

It is the servants who save him. They come close and reason with him gently: "My father, if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it? how much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?" (2 Kings 5:13). You would have paid any fortune, marched any distance, performed any feat. The hardness is not the difficulty of the command. The hardness is its plainness. It asks nothing of your greatness and everything of your pride.

And he bends. "Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean" (2 Kings 5:14). Like a little child. The commander goes down into the despised river a leper and comes up new, with the skin of a child, with nothing to boast of except a God who heals the ones who stop demanding to heal themselves. He goes back to confess that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel — the very God his nation's neighbor would not consult.

**The greed that grabs what was given free**

But the chapter does not end clean, and we must not pretend it does. Naaman offers payment and Elisha refuses every coin — grace is grace, and it cannot be sold. Then Gehazi, the prophet's own servant, who watched the whole thing, runs after the Syrian and lies to get the silver and the garments his master gave away. He grabs for what was given freely. And he comes back to a prophet who saw it all, and the word lands like a verdict: "The leprosy therefore of Naaman shall cleave unto thee, and unto thy seed for ever. And he went out from his presence a leper as white as snow" (2 Kings 5:27).

Turn the mirror. The pagan commander is healed; the prophet's insider is condemned. The outsider receives grace as a gift; the insider tries to monetize it and carries the disease out the door. I have stood closer to the things of God than Naaman ever did and reached, like Gehazi, to make grace pay me something — a reputation, a hold over people, a quiet fee for handling holy things. The man who has been near the prophet his whole life can still grab for the silver and walk home a leper.

This is the warning hanging over the whole book. Israel had the temple, the prophets, the covenant — and treated grace as a commodity and themselves as exempt, and the leprosy of judgment cleaved to them while the door stood open to nations they despised. Grace offends the proud and corrupts the grasping, and only heals the one who goes down into the water with empty hands. "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God" (Ephesians 2:8). The Jordan that washed a leper clean runs to a greater washing, where the Son of David would go down into our death seven times over and rise with flesh made new for everyone who quits buying and simply obeys, "Wash, and be clean."

Grace offends before it heals.

## The Hills Are Full of Fire
*The unseen armies of God, and the night a starving city ate the enemy's bread*

**Text:** 2 Kings 6–7 · **Supporting:** 2 Kings 6:16 · 2 Kings 6:17 · 2 Kings 7:9 · 2 Corinthians 4:18

The servant of the prophet rose early, went out, and saw the city ringed with horses and chariots and a great army of Syria. And his heart failed him. "Alas, my master, how shall we do?" (2 Kings 6:15). It is the oldest question of fear, and it is asked by a man looking at exactly what is there. The army was real. The encirclement was real. The terror was reasonable. He simply could not see the half of the picture that mattered most.

**The eyes that were opened**

Elisha is not afraid, and his answer to his shaking servant is the line the whole passage hangs on: "Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them" (2 Kings 6:16). On the face of it, that is absurd. There are two of them and a hillside of cavalry. But the prophet is not counting the way the servant counts. And then he prays the prayer every frightened believer needs prayed over him: "LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see. And the LORD opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha" (2 Kings 6:17).

Notice what the miracle is and is not. God does not send the chariots of fire in answer to the prayer. The chariots were already there. The prayer is not "send help" but "open his eyes" — let him see the help that has surrounded him the entire time. The servant's problem was never the size of the enemy. It was the smallness of his sight. He was living in a world half-reported to him by his own fear, counting the visible army and blind to the armies of the LORD on the same hill.

This is the spiritual condition of every anxious saint, and I know it from the inside. I have stood in my study at two in the morning doing the math of my fears — the threat real, the encirclement real — and never once thought to ask God to open my eyes to the half of reality I could not see. The hills were full of fire and I was counting horses.

**The night the siege broke without a sword**

The eyes-that-see comes back doubled in chapter seven. Samaria is under siege so brutal that mothers are eating their own children, and a royal officer scoffs when Elisha promises that tomorrow flour will sell cheap in the gate — there is no earthly mechanism for it, and the man says so. Meanwhile four lepers sit at the gate, the most expendable men alive, reasoning that they will die whether they stay or surrender, so they might as well walk into the enemy camp.

And they walk into a miracle. "For the LORD had made the host of the Syrians to hear a noise of chariots, and a noise of horses, even the noise of a great host" (2 Kings 7:6). The same chariots of fire the servant finally saw, the Syrians heard — and fled in the night, leaving their tents, their silver, their food, their horses. The lepers stumble into abandoned plenty. The God who is more than the armies against you can break a siege overnight with a sound no human army made.

Then the lepers stop in the middle of their feasting and speak a sentence that turns the chapter into a charge: "We do not well: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace" (2 Kings 7:9). Good news this large cannot be hoarded. They go and tell the gatekeepers, the city pours out, the prophecy is fulfilled to the letter, and the scoffing officer is trampled in the gate, seeing the deliverance but never tasting it — exactly as the word had said.

**More are with you than against you**

So turn around. We spend our days counting the visible army — the diagnosis, the layoff, the wayward child, the shrinking church, the hostile culture — and we do the math of despair because we are looking at a world half-reported by our fear. The God of 2 Kings does not always remove the army. He opens the eyes. He shows the believer that the deciding forces in the universe are not the ones making the most noise on the hill. "We look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal" (2 Corinthians 4:18).

And here is the weight, because this is a book about a kingdom that fell. These chapters of fiery rescue sit inside a story marching toward exile, and that is not a contradiction — it is mercy. God kept showing this faithless people that He was more than every army arrayed against them, kept breaking sieges they had no right to survive, long after they had stopped trusting Him. The judgment that finally fell on Samaria was never because the LORD lacked chariots of fire. It was because they would not have their eyes opened.

The four lepers carrying good news out of an abandoned camp run straight to an empty tomb, where the most expendable witnesses — women, fishermen, a crucified rabbi's failures — would stumble into deliverance won by no sword of theirs and run to tell a starving world. The Son of David broke the siege of death in a night, and to sit on news that large is to do what is not well. The hills are still full of fire. Ask Him to open your eyes.

More are with you than against.

## The Sword of Judgment and Its Own Half Heart
*Jehu does exactly what God decreed against the house of Ahab — and keeps a sin of his own*

**Text:** 2 Kings 8–10 · **Supporting:** 1 Kings 21:21 · 2 Kings 10:16 · 2 Kings 10:29 · 2 Kings 10:31

The word spoken against the house of Ahab had been hanging in the air for years. Through the murder of Naboth, through Elijah's verdict in the vineyard, through the death of Ahab himself, the sentence waited: this house will be cut off, this dynasty will end, the blood of the prophets will be answered. And in these chapters the sword finally falls, carried by a hard-riding man named Jehu, who does exactly what God decreed — and then stops short of the one thing that would have made him whole.

**The word comes due**

A young prophet is sent to anoint Jehu in secret, pours oil on his head, and announces the commission: "thou shalt smite the house of Ahab thy master, that I may avenge the blood of my servants the prophets" (2 Kings 9:7). This is not Jehu's ambition. It is the LORD keeping an old promise, the one Elijah carried into Naboth's stolen vineyard: "I will take away thy posterity" (1 Kings 21:21). The judgment that lands here is not random political violence. It is covenant faithfulness with a sword in its hand.

And Jehu rides. He drives furiously, the text says, and the watchman knows him by the madness of his driving. He cuts down Joram in the very field of Naboth, so that the murdered man's blood is answered on his own murderer's ground. He kills Ahaziah of Judah. He rides into Jezreel and calls up to the window where Jezebel has painted her face and dressed her hair, and her own eunuchs throw her down, and the dogs eat her in the street, exactly as Elijah had said. He gathers the seventy sons of Ahab and ends the line. The narrator is unflinching: the LORD had spoken this, and it came to pass. God said it would happen, and it happened.

Then Jehu turns on Baal himself. He gathers all the worshipers into the temple of Baal under a pretense, packs the house, and puts every one of them to the sword, and tears down the image, and makes the temple of Baal a latrine in Israel. He is zealous, and he knows it, and he says so: "Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD" (2 Kings 10:16). The man is a flame against the idolatry of Ahab's house.

**The sin the executioner kept**

And here the chapter turns the knife on its own hero. For all his zeal, all his furious obedience, all the Baal-blood on his hands, there is a line Jehu will not cross. "Howbeit from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin, Jehu departed not from after them, to wit, the golden calves that were in Bethel, and that were in Dan" (2 Kings 10:29). He destroyed the foreign god and kept the homegrown one. He tore down Baal and left the golden calves standing — the older, more comfortable, more politically useful idolatry that had been Israel's national sin since the kingdom split.

The verdict on him is precise and devastating: "But Jehu took no heed to walk in the law of the LORD God of Israel with all his heart: for he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam" (2 Kings 10:31). He was zealous against the sin that was easy to hate and untroubled by the sin that served his throne. The golden calves were not foreign. They were Israel's own, set up generations earlier so the northern kingdom would not have to send its people south to worship in Jerusalem. They were political infrastructure. To tear them down would have weakened Jehu's own grip on the throne he had just bloodied his way onto — and so they stayed. His reform went exactly as far as his self-interest allowed and not one step further. He was the executioner of one idolatry and the patron of another, and he never seems to have felt the contradiction.

**Zeal that is not yet obedience**

Turn the mirror around, slowly, because this one is uncomfortably close. We are very good at zeal against the sins we already despise — the ones that belong to the other tribe, the other party, the people we were never tempted to be. We torch the Baal we never worshiped and keep the golden calf we cannot afford to lose. I have stood in a pulpit white-hot against the idols of the people across the aisle and walked home to my own quiet calves at Bethel and Dan, untroubled, because mine were useful to me. Jehu is not a stranger. Jehu is the religious man's most flattering disguise — the executioner of other people's sins.

This is the warning the book is building toward. Israel had reformers. Israel had zeal. What Israel did not have was a heart that would surrender the comfortable idol along with the foreign one, and so the kingdom went on rotting under kings who attacked sin selectively until the whole house came down. Zeal against an enemy's idol is not the same as obedience with the whole heart. God measures the second.

And that exposes our need for a King the book cannot supply. Every son of David and every captain of Israel keeps his own golden calf, reforms in part, obeys with a divided heart, and leaves a sin standing that judgment will one day answer. The half-hearted executioner points past himself to the one King who would not depart from the law of the LORD in anything — who tore down every idol including the ones that served Him, who obeyed with His whole heart down into an exile He did not earn, so that half-hearted reformers like Jehu and like us could be made new from the inside. The sword in our hand against another man's idol saves no one. Only a clean heart will do, and only Christ can give it.

Zeal is not yet obedience.

## A Hidden Child and the Arrows Struck Too Few
*David's lamp not put out, and the deliverance forfeited by a king who stopped too soon*

**Text:** 2 Kings 11–13 · **Supporting:** 2 Kings 11:2 · 2 Samuel 7:16 · 2 Kings 13:18 · 2 Kings 13:19

When Athaliah saw that her son was dead, she rose and destroyed all the royal seed. The queen mother of Judah set out to murder her own grandchildren to seize the throne, and she very nearly succeeded. For one moment in the long story of David's line, the lamp of the house of David flickered down to almost nothing — one infant standing between an old promise and total dark.

**The child hidden in the house of God**

But the verb in the text is not "killed." It is "stole." "Jehosheba... took Joash the son of Ahaziah, and stole him from among the king's sons which were slain; and they hid him... in the bedchamber from Athaliah, so that he was not slain" (2 Kings 11:2). One aunt, one baby, one bedchamber in the temple. For six years the rightful king of Judah is hidden in the house of the LORD while a usurper sits the throne, and the promise of God to David survives in a nursery no one can see.

This is the quiet engine of the whole book. God had sworn to David, "thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever" (2 Samuel 7:16). Athaliah's sword is aimed straight at that promise — whether she knows it or not — and the promise does not die, because God keeps a child alive in the dark when every visible sign says the line is finished. Notice how thin the thread is. Not an army between Athaliah and the end of David's house. Not a rival claimant with soldiers. One woman with the nerve to steal a baby and one room in the temple where a usurper would not think to look. That is how God guards His promise here — not with visible power, but with a hidden child and a faithful aunt, so that no one could ever say David's line survived by its own strength. In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada brings the boy out, crowns him, and the people clap their hands and shout, "God save the king." Athaliah cries treason and is put to death, the covenant is renewed between the LORD and the king and the people, the altars of Baal are torn down, and the house of the LORD is repaired with money laid in a chest by the door. A child hidden becomes a king restored, and David's lamp burns again.

**The arrows struck too few**

But the same span of chapters that shows the lamp preserved also shows how easily deliverance is half-taken. The good is fragile here. When Jehoiada the priest dies, Joash himself drifts, and the reform he led does not outlive the man who held his hand. And then comes one of the strangest, saddest scenes in the book.

Elisha is dying, and the king of Israel, Joash, comes to his bedside weeping. The prophet has the king take a bow and arrows, lays his own hands on the king's hands, and tells him to shoot eastward — "The arrow of the LORD's deliverance" (2 Kings 13:17). Then he tells him to take the arrows and strike the ground. And the king strikes three times and stops. "And the man of God was wroth with him, and said, Thou shouldest have smitten five or six times; then hadst thou smitten Syria till thou hadst consumed it: whereas now thou shalt smite Syria but thrice" (2 Kings 13:19).

He stopped too soon. The deliverance was offered in full and taken in part. There was nothing in the room rationing the victory — only a king who struck the ground a few polite times and quit, who treated the promise of God as a formality to get through rather than a flood to throw himself into. The arrows were in his hand. The limit on his deliverance was set by his own half-hearted reach.

**Half measures forfeit full deliverance**

Now turn it on us, because both halves of this passage are our story. We are saved by a grace that hides a child in the dark and keeps a promise alive when we have no part in keeping it — that side is pure gift, and we contribute nothing to it but the danger. And we are also Joash with the arrows, forever striking the ground three times when God said keep striking. We pray until we are slightly less afraid and stop. We forgive until it is awkward and stop. We obey up to the edge of comfort and stop, and then we wonder why the victory in our lives is partial, and we blame the bow.

I have struck the ground three times more often than I can count. I have asked God for exactly as much deliverance as would let me keep my life otherwise unchanged, and then mistaken my own small reach for the limit of His arm. The prophet's anger at the bedside is grief, not rage — the grief of watching a man forfeit what was freely offered because he would not strike one more time.

This is the book's double warning and its double comfort. The kingdom is falling because king after king takes the covenant in part — strikes three times, keeps the calves, lets the reform die with the priest. And yet the lamp is not put out, because the survival of David's house never depended on the kings' whole hearts in the first place. The child stolen from the slaughter and hidden in the temple points to a greater Son of David who would be hunted from birth by a jealous king and hidden until His hour, the lamp that no Athaliah and no exile and no grave could extinguish. He struck the ground not three times but to the last, consuming our enemy entirely, taking the full deliverance that we were always too half-hearted to seize. Strike like a man who believes the promise.

Half measures forfeit full deliverance.

## Why Samaria Fell
*The long indictment of the north, and a God who warned for two hundred years*

**Text:** 2 Kings 14–17 · **Supporting:** 2 Kings 17:13 · 2 Kings 17:14 · 2 Kings 17:18 · 2 Kings 17:23

For four chapters the kings of the north come and go like a procession of the doomed. Jeroboam, Zechariah, Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah, Pekah, Hoshea — names you forget as fast as you read them, and that forgettableness is the point. They share one obituary, written again and again with almost no variation: he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD; he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam, who made Israel to sin. Then Assyria comes, and the northern kingdom is carried away, and the book stops the story to tell us why.

**The long patience before the fall**

The fall of Samaria looks sudden — a siege, a deportation, a kingdom erased in a generation. But the narrator refuses to let us read it as a recent accident. He traces the whole arc backward, and it does not start with Assyria's armies. It starts with golden calves set up two centuries earlier, with a national sin handed down from father to son for nineteen kings, with a patience on God's part that is almost unbearable to read about. "Yet the LORD testified against Israel, and against Judah, by all the prophets, and by all the seers, saying, Turn ye from your evil ways, and keep my commandments" (2 Kings 17:13).

By all the prophets. By all the seers. For generation after generation. Elijah, Elisha, and the named and unnamed messengers who kept coming with the same word — turn, keep covenant, come home — until the patience itself became a kind of testimony against a people who would not hear. This is the thing we get wrong about the judgment of God. We imagine a short fuse. The text shows a God so slow to anger that He sent prophet after prophet across two hundred years to a kingdom that murdered the prophets and kept the calves.

**The verdict the narrator will not soften**

And then the writer does something unusual. He stops the action entirely and delivers the verdict in plain prose, so that no reader can mistake the deportation for bad luck or imperial politics. "Notwithstanding they would not hear, but hardened their necks, like to the neck of their fathers, that did not believe in the LORD their God" (2 Kings 17:14). The same neck as their fathers. The same unbelief, inherited and chosen, generation laid on generation.

The harvest is named without flinching: "Therefore the LORD was very angry with Israel, and removed them out of his sight: there was none left but the tribe of Judah only" (2 Kings 17:18). And again, so it cannot be missed: "So was Israel carried away out of their own land to Assyria unto this day" (2 Kings 17:23). This is not a tragedy that befell Israel. It is a sentence Israel was warned of from the very giving of the covenant — that to break faith with the LORD was to be vomited out of the land — and the warning ran its full course before it fell. God told them what would happen. They would not hear. It happened.

This is the theological spine of the entire book of 2 Kings standing up to speak in its own voice. Covenant judgment is not random tragedy. It is the keeping of an old promise, and the promise had a curse-side that the prophets quoted to their faces for ten generations. The exile is terrible precisely because it is not arbitrary.

**God warned them — and warns us**

Now turn around, because the long-suffering of God toward Israel is the thing we are most tempted to presume upon ourselves. We read these chapters as the story of those people back then, the obviously wicked north, the kings with the forgettable names. But the narrator's whole method is to slow down and show that the fall was the fruit of a patience abused — a God who kept sending the word long after they stopped listening, a people who hardened the same neck their fathers hardened and called it normal.

I have hardened my neck against words I knew were from God and mistaken the silence afterward for permission. I have treated His patience as His indifference, and so have we, congregation after congregation that hears the same warning year after year and changes nothing, certain that grace this long must mean a judgment that never comes. Samaria believed that too. The kindness of God that should lead us to repentance, we read as proof that repentance can wait.

And yet — hold this — even in the verdict there is a thread of mercy the narrator slips in: "there was none left but the tribe of Judah only." The northern lamp goes out, but the southern lamp, the lamp of David, still burns. The patience that ran out on Samaria has not yet run out on the line that carries the promise. The God who warned for two hundred years and finally let Assyria come is the same God keeping one tribe alive to bring the King.

That King would stand over a city like Jerusalem and weep that it would not hear the prophets either — that He, the last and greatest word sent to a neck-hardened people, would be murdered like the seers before Him. And then He would take into His own body the curse-side of the covenant we all earned, carried away out of God's sight on a cross so that a hardened, deserving people could be brought home. God is still sending the word. The patience is real, and it is not endless. Hear Him while He calls.

God warned them. They would not hear.

## He Defends His City for His Own Name
*Hezekiah spreads the blasphemy before God — and the same king parades his treasure*

**Text:** 2 Kings 18–20 · **Supporting:** 2 Kings 19:14 · 2 Kings 19:34 · 2 Kings 19:35 · 2 Kings 20:17

Sennacherib, king of Assyria, had already swallowed the northern kingdom and was eating his way through the fortified cities of Judah. His field commander stood outside the wall of Jerusalem and shouted in the language of the people, so the men on the wall would hear and lose heart: where are the gods of the nations I have already destroyed? Why should your God be any different? Do not let Hezekiah deceive you. The threat was credible. The empire was real. And the blasphemy was aimed straight at the name of the LORD.

**The letter spread before the LORD**

Then Sennacherib put it in writing. A letter came demanding surrender and mocking the God of Israel as one more local deity about to be added to Assyria's collection. And here is the moment the whole passage turns on — what a believing king does with a letter full of blasphemy: "And Hezekiah received the letter of the hand of the messengers, and read it: and Hezekiah went up into the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD" (2 Kings 19:14).

He did not answer the commander. He did not call a council of war. He did not send for Egypt's chariots, the reflex of every faithless king in this book. He took the threat to the temple, opened it before God, and prayed — and the heart of his prayer is not "save us because we are worth saving." It is this: "Now therefore, O LORD our God, I beseech thee, save thou us out of his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that thou art the LORD God, even thou only" (2 Kings 19:19). Save us for the sake of who You are. Let the watching nations learn that the God they thought was one more idol is the only God there is.

This is the right way to carry a terror. Not to deny it, not to manage it alone, not to run to Egypt, but to spread it open before the One whose name is on the line. Hezekiah understood that his city's danger was a question about God's reputation, and he laid it where it belonged.

**The angel and the empty camp**

And God answered through Isaiah with a promise rooted not in Judah's strength but in His own commitment: "For I will defend this city, to save it, for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake" (2 Kings 19:34). For mine own sake. The deliverance, when it comes, will be a defense of the name that the Assyrian dared to mock and a keeping of the promise made to David's house.

Then the most one-sided battle in Scripture: "And it came to pass that night, that the angel of the LORD went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses" (2 Kings 19:35). No sword of Judah was lifted. No arrow was loosed from the wall. The mightiest army on earth simply did not wake up, and Sennacherib went home and was cut down by his own sons in the temple of his own god. The God who would not be consulted as one among many had just answered the empire that called Him one among many. He defended His city, and He did it for His own name.

**He saves the city — and names the future**

But the chapters do not let us close the book on a hero. The same Hezekiah, struck with mortal illness, is given fifteen added years and a sign — and then, when envoys come from rising Babylon, he shows them everything. All his treasure, all his armory, all his house. He parades the glory of Judah before the next empire, and Isaiah comes with a harder word than the one against Assyria: "Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house... shall be carried into Babylon: nothing shall be left" (2 Kings 20:17). The city God just defended is told, in the same breath, where its sons will one day go.

Turn around. We are quick to be Hezekiah at the wall, spreading our crisis before God in the emergency, and slow to see ourselves in Hezekiah at the window, showing off the treasure once the danger has passed. The same man who prayed so well in the siege grew careless in the peace, and his carelessness seeded the next exile. I have prayed like a saint in the crisis and lived like a fool in the safety afterward, and I suspect the church does this on a national scale — desperate before God when the empire is at the gate, and proud of its own treasure the moment the threat lifts.

This is the bittersweet honesty of the book. God really does defend His city, by sheer grace, for His own name's sake, with no help from us. And the deliverance does not cure the heart of the man delivered, and the seeds of the coming judgment are already in the house even as the angel clears the field. Salvation by grace and the long arc of judgment stand side by side in one king's life.

And both point past Hezekiah. The city defended for the LORD's own name and David's sake points to a greater Son of David, whose city would not be spared the sword but who would Himself become the defense — taking the blasphemy and the siege and the exile into His own body, dying outside the wall so that a far more deserving judgment could pass over a people who, like Hezekiah, pray well and live badly. God still saves for His own name's sake. He still names the future we would rather not hear.

He saves the city, names the future.

## When the Book Was Found
*Manasseh's blood, Josiah's torn robe, and the reform that could not reverse the verdict*

**Text:** 2 Kings 21–23 · **Supporting:** 2 Kings 21:16 · 2 Kings 22:11 · 2 Kings 22:13 · 2 Kings 23:25

Before there is a hero in these chapters, there is a horror. Manasseh reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem and did more evil than the nations God had driven out before Israel. He rebuilt the high places his father tore down, set up altars to Baal in the house of the LORD itself, passed his own son through the fire, dealt in sorcery, and seduced Judah to do worse than the Canaanites. And then this: "Moreover Manasseh shed innocent blood very much, till he had filled Jerusalem from one end to another" (2 Kings 21:16). A city filled with blood, end to end. That is the soil the next reform grows in.

**The sentence set beyond recall**

The text is unsparing about what Manasseh's reign did. The LORD speaks through the prophets that He will bring evil on Jerusalem and Judah, that He will wipe the city as a man wipes a dish and turns it upside down, that He will forsake the remnant of His inheritance. The accumulated guilt of generations, brought to its full weight under Manasseh, sets the sentence on Jerusalem beyond recall. The verdict is fixed before the reformer is born. Whatever good is coming, it will arrive too late to reverse what an earlier generation made certain.

We need to feel that before we meet Josiah, because it changes everything about how we read him. His reform is not going to be a story of a good king who fixed it in time. It is going to be a story of a good king who did everything right and could not undo the harvest already planted — and was good anyway.

**The book that tore a king's robes**

Josiah comes to the throne as a boy, and in the eighteenth year of his reign, while repairing the temple, the high priest finds something that had been lost: the book of the law. They bring it and read it to the king, and the response is the hinge of the whole passage: "And it came to pass, when the king had heard the words of the book of the law, that he rent his clothes" (2 Kings 22:11).

He tore his robes. Not because the book told him something new, but because it told him the truth about how far his nation had wandered, and he did not flinch from it or explain it away. His next words show a man undone by what he heard: "Great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book" (2 Kings 22:13). He inquires of the LORD, and the prophetess Huldah confirms it — the evil is coming, the sentence stands — but because his heart was tender and he humbled himself and wept, he himself will be gathered to his grave in peace before the disaster falls.

And then Josiah does the most thorough reform in the history of Judah, knowing it will not reverse the verdict. He gathers the people and reads them the covenant. He tears down the altars in the house of the LORD, burns the vessels made for Baal, defiles the high places from Geba to Beersheba, breaks the houses of the cult prostitutes, destroys the altar at Bethel that Jeroboam built two hundred years before, and keeps a Passover such as had not been kept since the days of the judges. The verdict on him is the highest in the book: "And like unto him was there no king before him, that turned to the LORD with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses" (2 Kings 23:25). With all his heart. The thing Jehu lacked. The thing Joash forfeited. Josiah had it — and the exile came anyway.

**Repentance that matters even when it costs**

Turn it on us, because here is where we are tempted to a quiet cynicism. If the reform could not stop the judgment, why tear the robes at all? Why repent if repentance does not reverse the verdict? We are practical people. We want our obedience to pay. And the moment we discover that a sin's consequences will fall regardless — the marriage already broken, the years already lost, the harvest of an earlier choice already coming — something in us asks what the point of repenting now could possibly be.

The book answers by simply showing us Josiah, and refusing to apologize for him. His repentance was real and it was good and it was right, and God saw it and honored it and spared the man even while the nation fell. Tearing the robes was not a failed lever to move God's hand. It was the only fitting response of a true heart to the truth about itself, whether or not it changed the outcome. I have wanted my repentance to buy back the consequence, and when it could not, I have been tempted to skip it — to harden where Josiah tore his clothes, because softening seemed to gain me nothing. That is the calculus of a man who repents to manage outcomes rather than because the LORD is holy and he is not.

This is the painful grace at the center of the book. Repentance does not always reverse the harvest. The exile that Manasseh's generation guaranteed came on Josiah's good and grieving people. And yet God meets the tender heart with mercy inside the judgment, gathers His servant in peace, honors a turning that changed no policy in heaven's court but changed everything in the man.

The lost book that broke a king's heart points to a greater word made flesh, who would also weep over Jerusalem and tear nothing of His own but be Himself torn — the King who turned to the LORD with all His heart and all His soul and all His might, and bore the verdict that no reform could reverse, so that our repentance, which can never buy back the consequence, is met by a grace that can. Tear your robes even when it costs you nothing you can see. The LORD is near the broken heart.

Repentance matters even when it costs.

## The Gate Is Broken, the Lamp Still Burns
*The temple in ashes, the king's eyes put out — and a strange mercy at a foreign table*

**Text:** 2 Kings 24–25 · **Supporting:** 2 Kings 25:9 · 2 Kings 24:3 · 2 Kings 25:29 · 2 Samuel 7:16

It ends the way the prophets said it would. Babylon comes up against Jerusalem, the wall is breached, the city is starved into surrender, and Zedekiah runs in the night and is caught in the plains of Jericho. They kill his sons before his eyes, and then put out his eyes, so that the last thing the last king of Judah ever saw was the end of his own line. He is bound in chains and carried to Babylon. The kingdom that began with David's throne ends with a blind king stumbling into exile.

**The temple in ashes**

And then the fire. The captain of the guard comes and burns it all: "And he burnt the house of the LORD, and the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and every great man's house burnt he with fire" (2 Kings 25:9). The temple — Solomon's temple, the house where the glory of the LORD had filled the holy place, the center of Israel's whole life with God — is reduced to ash and broken bronze carried off as scrap. The walls of Jerusalem are pulled down. The people are taken away. The land is left to the poorest of the poor.

This is the disaster the entire book has been walking toward, slowly, for twenty-five chapters. And the narrator will not let us read it as the triumph of a stronger empire. He has been telling us all along that this was covenant judgment, not political accident: "Surely at the commandment of the LORD came this upon Judah, to remove them out of his sight, for the sins of Manasseh" (2 Kings 24:3). God said it would happen, through prophet after prophet, for generation after generation. They would not hear. And now it has happened, exactly, to the letter. The fire in the temple is the keeping of an old, old promise — the curse-side of a covenant they swore at Sinai and broke for centuries.

We are tempted to flinch from this, to soften the judgment into mere consequence or imperial misfortune. The book will not let us. It insists, in plain prose, that the God of Israel was not absent when His house burned. He was keeping His word. That is harder than abandonment, and truer.

**A strange mercy at the king's table**

And then, in the last paragraph of the book, after the fire and the blinding and the chains, something turns. The story does not end in total dark. Years pass in Babylon, and a new king of Babylon comes to the throne, and he does an inexplicable thing. He brings Jehoiachin, the exiled king of Judah, out of prison: "And he spake kindly to him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings that were with him in Babylon... and he did eat bread continually before him all the days of his life" (2 Kings 25:28–29).

A son of David, lifted from a dungeon, given clean clothes and a changed garment and a seat at the king's table, eating bread before the king all the days of his life. It is an undeserved kindness, small and strange and easy to miss, and it is the last thing the book chooses to tell us. Why end here? Because as long as a son of David is alive and eating bread, David's lamp is not put out. The promise still breathes. "Thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever" (2 Samuel 7:16) — and judgment, for all its fury, did not extinguish it. The gate is broken. The lamp still burns.

**Judgment fell, and the promise held**

Turn around, because we are the people who need both halves of this ending and usually want only one. We want the lamp without the fire — a God who forgives without judging, a covenant with no curse-side, a Christianity where sin never burns anything down. And the book of 2 Kings, in its last chapter, refuses us that. The temple really burned. The judgment was real, deserved, and exactly as the word had promised. There is no reading of this book where covenant unfaithfulness costs nothing.

But we are also the people who, having finally felt the weight of the fire, are tempted to despair — to believe that when the consequences fall, when the marriage ends or the years are lost or the church we loved goes into its own kind of exile, God's promises have failed and the dark has won. And the book refuses us that too. The very last image is not the smoke over Jerusalem. It is a son of David eating bread at a table in a far country, kept alive by a mercy he did not earn.

I have stood in the rubble of things I helped burn down and assumed the lamp was out, that the promise had run through my fingers along with the consequence. That is reading the book one chapter short. Judgment fell — and the promise held. Both. At once. From the same hand.

That ember of grace at a foreign table points past every failed king to the Son of David who would go into the deepest exile of all — not merely carried from His land but cut off from the face of God, His own eyes closing in a darkness He did not earn, His own body broken like the gate of the city. He went into our exile so that He could bring us out of it, and rose to keep a throne that no Babylon and no grave could touch. The temple of His body was torn down and raised in three days, and now He sets His exiled people at the King's table to eat bread before Him all the days of their lives. If you are sitting in the ashes of a deserved judgment, look once more at the last paragraph. The gate is broken. The lamp still burns.

Judgment fell. The promise held.
